strengths: Addresses an important problem: improving the security of generated code without requiring model fine-tuning or sacrificing functional correctness.
The combination of summarized security guidance, security-focused code slicing, and hierarchical multi-faceted retrieval is a sensible and practically useful system design.
The evaluation covers six diverse language models and compares against five baselines spanning retrieval, fine-tuning, constrained decoding, tool-assisted refinement, and multi-agent approaches.
The paper reports substantial SecurePass@1 gains on CodeGuard+ and includes useful component ablations, functional-correctness benchmarks, and latency/token analyses.
weaknesses: Security effectiveness is evaluated on only one small benchmark with 94 scenarios. HumanEval+, BigCodeBench, and LiveCodeBench measure functionality but provide no independent evidence of security generalization.

The authors select k and apparently the retrieval thresholds using CodeGuard+ itself, yet report final performance on the same benchmark. Without a held-out validation split, this introduces test-set tuning and weakens the central empirical claim.

The claimed generalization to unseen CWE types is unsupported: Table 8 only counts CWE coverage and does not report performance separately on seen versus unseen types. Because retrieval traverses CWE nodes present in the knowledge base, this omission is especially important.

The program-slicing component is insufficiently specified and potentially inconsistent. Tree-sitter alone does not provide the semantic data/control dependencies needed for a reliable PDG, while the pseudocode excludes zero-length paths and thus appears not to include the patch points themselves. Cross-version alignment and the stated context-completion procedure are also undefined.

Several conclusions overstate the ablations. In Table 3, using all three facets is not best on most individual metric/model combinations; vulnerability-cause retrieval alone is best for both security metrics on Qwen. Table 4 omits the GPT-4o summarization results needed to substantiate its claim of comparable performance.

No confidence intervals, significance tests, or per-CWE/task breakdowns are provided. Consequently, it is unclear whether several modest improvements are robust across tasks rather than driven by a subset of scenarios.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of released knowledge-base artifacts or code and by missing implementation details for PDG construction, threshold selection, score normalization, retrieval indexing, and vulnerability-cause model calls. Potential overlap between the SafeCoder-derived knowledge base and CodeGuard+ is not audited.

The method requires multiple LLM calls and roughly doubles or triples online generation latency. Although latency is reported, cost-normalized comparisons and simpler prompt-only or equal-call-budget baselines are missing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving the security of LLM-generated code without model fine-tuning.

RESCUE combines knowledge distillation, program slicing, and multi-faceted retrieval in a coherent framework. Using vulnerability causes, API patterns, and draft-code similarity is intuitively well motivated.
The experimental scope is broad on paper, covering six LLMs, five baseline methods, four benchmarks, and several component ablations.
SecurePass@1 is a sensible joint metric because it avoids rewarding code that is secure only because it is nonfunctional.
weaknesses: The central evaluation relies on only one security benchmark with 94 scenarios. HumanEval+, BigCodeBench, and LiveCodeBench measure functionality but provide no additional evidence of security improvements, substantially limiting the claimed generality.

The experimental protocol appears to tune the method on the reported CodeGuard+ evaluation set: Figure 3 varies k on CodeGuard+ and explicitly selects k=4 from those results for all experiments. The provenance and tuning data for the three retrieval thresholds are not reported. This creates a serious risk of test-set overfitting.

The comparisons do not isolate retrieval from additional inference compute. RESCUE performs draft generation, vulnerability-cause analysis, and final generation, yet there is no comparable-compute baseline that feeds the model its own security analysis, uses explicit secure-coding prompting, performs self-refinement, or samples multiple candidates. Consequently, improvements cannot confidently be attributed to the proposed knowledge base and retrieval machinery.

Several baseline adaptations are insufficiently justified. Codexity's analysis tool is replaced, implementations of INDICT and SafeCoder are described only briefly, and their very large functionality collapses suggest possible sensitivity to implementation or prompting. No validation against published baseline results is supplied.

No confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, run-to-run variation, or per-problem paired analysis are reported. With temperature-based sampling and many samples from only 94 tasks, treating sample-level observations as independent could greatly overstate evidential strength.

The program-slicing method is under-specified and internally inconsistent. Algorithm 2 includes only nodes connected to a point of interest by paths of length at least one, apparently omitting the point-of-interest statement itself. It also does not formalize the claimed cross-version comparison and context-completion step. How tree-sitter alone supports sound data/control-dependence graphs for Python and C/C++, including aliasing and interprocedural behavior, is unexplained.

The generalization claim from unseen CWE counts is unsupported. The paper provides no security performance broken down by seen versus unseen CWE, language, vulnerability class, or scenario, so Table 8 alone cannot demonstrate generalization.

Retrieval quality is never evaluated directly. There is no annotated relevance assessment, CWE-selection accuracy, oracle-retrieval comparison, qualitative failure analysis, or evidence that retrieved examples correspond to the vulnerabilities actually tested.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the central results: no code or constructed knowledge base is provided; the offline vulnerability-cause summarization prompt appears missing; threshold-selection procedures, random seeds, exact checkpoint identifiers, indexing details, and several decoding parameters are absent. Some prompt templates also contain ambiguous or malformed fencing and labels.

The cost analysis understates overhead by discussing acceptability without a normalized end-to-end comparison. RESCUE requires multiple LLM calls and roughly doubles or triples latency in the reported examples, while the token analysis counts only augmented-generation inputs and omits preliminary calls.

Some conclusions are stronger than the tables support. For example, the full three-facet configuration is not best for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, and the assertion that broader CWE coverage demonstrates generalization does not follow from the reported evidence. Overall, the idea is promising, but the evaluation design and technical specification are not reliable enough for acceptance at a top-tier venue. strengths: RESCUE is well motivated and combines hierarchical security-knowledge construction, program slicing, and multi-faceted retrieval into a coherent framework tailored to secure code generation.

The evaluation is broad in model coverage: six LLMs from several families are compared with five representative baselines spanning RAG, fine-tuning, constrained decoding, tool-based repair, and agentic critique.

The main security results are consistently favorable. RESCUE improves SecurePass@1 over the base models by 6.28 percentage points on average and reportedly exceeds the strongest baseline by 4.8 points, while generally retaining useful functional performance.

The paper includes valuable component-level evidence: knowledge-base ablations, all seven combinations of retrieval facets, hierarchy/top-k analysis, alternative summarization models, slicing-length measurements, and latency breakdowns.

SecurePass@k is a sensible joint measure that avoids rewarding nonfunctional programs merely for passing a security checker. The use of a different tool during baseline generation also helps reduce direct leakage from the CodeQL evaluator.
The paper is clearly structured, and its central design choices are intuitive and relevant to practical secure-code generation.
weaknesses: The security evidence rests almost entirely on CodeGuard+, a benchmark of only 94 scenarios evaluated with static CodeQL checks. The other three benchmarks measure functionality only; there is no second security benchmark, dynamic exploit testing, expert assessment, or evaluation against vulnerabilities outside CodeQL's detection coverage.

There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, or per-task analyses. This matters because the headline differences are sometimes modest and the 100 samples generated per task are correlated rather than 9,400 independent evaluation units.

Hyperparameters appear to be selected using the same CodeGuard+ results ultimately reported: Figure 3 explicitly motivates k=4 from benchmark performance, while the provenance of the three retrieval thresholds is unclear. A held-out development set or robustness analysis is needed to avoid test-set tuning.

The generalization claim is insufficiently demonstrated. Counting CWE types absent from the training set does not establish success on them; results should be stratified by seen versus unseen CWE. The paper also does not report a task-, repository-, or patch-level overlap audit between the SafeCoder-derived knowledge base and CodeGuard+, leaving possible retrieval leakage unresolved.

Important implementation details are underspecified. Tree-sitter alone does not provide a full program-dependence graph, and the construction of data/control dependencies, cross-version statement matching, handling of incomplete programs, and the stated context-completion procedure are not described sufficiently for reproduction. Algorithm 2 also appears to exclude the slicing criterion itself by requiring path length of at least one.

The claim that functionality is preserved is somewhat overstated. RESCUE loses 3.63 points on BigCodeBench on average, including a 9.4-point drop for GPT-4o-mini, and also produces notable model-specific regressions on CodeGuard+ and HumanEval+. Tradeoffs should be presented more explicitly.

The method requires two preliminary LLM calls in addition to final generation. The reported timings imply roughly a threefold end-to-end latency increase, yet monetary cost, generated-token overhead, parallel execution measurements, and comparison-normalized costs are absent.

The conceptual novelty is moderate: the contribution is primarily an effective integration of summarization, slicing, hierarchical retrieval, multi-query retrieval, and rank fusion. The proposed SecurePass metric is useful but is essentially joint functional-and-security pass rate rather than a technically substantial metric contribution.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: improving the security of LLM-generated code without model fine-tuning or dependence on the evaluation-time security checker.

The proposed combination of hierarchical security knowledge, LLM-based guideline distillation, program slicing, and multi-faceted retrieval is coherent and more security-aware than conventional similarity-only RAG.
The empirical study is unusually broad, covering six LLMs, several competing method families, four principal benchmarks, and an additional dynamically evaluated CWEval benchmark.
SecurePass@k is a sensible metric because it requires generated programs to satisfy both functional and security tests, avoiding the misleading gains possible with SecureRate alone.
The component ablations, seen/unseen-CWE analysis, cross-language experiments, fusion comparison, and latency breakdown provide useful evidence beyond the headline result.
weaknesses: The main CodeGuard+ results are not cleanly separated from model selection. The paper chooses k from performance curves on CodeGuard+ and tunes retrieval thresholds using 20 sampled CodeGuard+ instances, but does not state that these instances were excluded from the final test results. This creates potential test-set leakage and weakens the central 4.8-point state-of-the-art claim.

No confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or task-level variance are reported. Generating 100 samples per task reduces sampling noise but does not address uncertainty across only 94 CodeGuard+ tasks; consequently, several small reported differences cannot be judged statistically reliable.

The program-analysis component is substantially underspecified. Tree-sitter is a parser rather than a complete PDG implementation, and the paper does not explain alias analysis, pointer handling, scope resolution, control dependence, or cross-function calls for Python and C/C++. Algorithm 2 also appears to exclude the points of interest themselves by requiring path lengths of at least one. These omissions impede assessment and reproduction of a central claimed innovation.

Baseline fairness is uncertain. Several reproduced baselines suffer very large functional regressions, while the manuscript provides limited implementation and tuning detail needed to establish faithful adaptations to the new model families. The external CWEval evaluation compares only against zero-shot and SecCoder, so it does not independently substantiate state-of-the-art performance over the stronger baseline set.

The functional-preservation claims are overstated. RESCUE loses 3.63 Pass@1 points on BigCodeBench on average, including a 9.4-point drop for GPT-4o-mini, and also reduces CodeGuard+ functional accuracy for several models. Reporting only an aggregate retention percentage obscures these material regressions.

The novelty is primarily an integration of established techniques—hierarchical summarization, bounded program slicing, multi-query retrieval, and thresholded reciprocal-rank fusion—rather than a major new learning or retrieval principle. The paper does not directly evaluate retrieval accuracy, making it difficult to verify the proposed explanation for downstream gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract ends with “Our code is available at” without a repository URL, despite the reproducibility statement referring to that link. Important details such as the resulting knowledge base, exact PDG construction, retrieved-item counts, empty-retrieval behavior, random seeds, and evaluation splits are also absent.

The overhead analysis reports component latency but omits a zero-shot latency baseline, token/API cost, and end-to-end throughput. RESCUE requires draft generation, vulnerability analysis, retrieval, and final generation, so its practical cost is more significant than the discussion suggests.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving the security of LLM-generated code without model fine-tuning or relying on a security analyzer during generation.

RESCUE is a coherent integration of hierarchical security knowledge, program slicing, proactive query construction, and multi-faceted retrieval. The motivation for filtering task-irrelevant code from retrieved examples is sensible.
The empirical study is broad in model coverage, with six LLMs, several competing secure-generation approaches, four primary benchmarks, and an additional dynamically tested security benchmark.

The authors report useful component analyses, including knowledge-base ablations, all combinations of retrieval facets, alternative summarization models, latency, seen versus unseen CWEs, cross-language transfer, and threshold sensitivity.
SecurePass@1 appropriately avoids rewarding outputs that are secure merely because they are functionally incorrect, exposing an important weakness of SecureRate-only comparisons.
The ethics discussion recognizes dual-use concerns, and the method is primarily defensive.
weaknesses: The central evaluation appears contaminated by model selection on the test benchmark. The authors vary the number of retrieved CWE nodes on CodeGuard+ and select k=4 based on the observed peak, while the retrieval thresholds are validated on 20 sampled CodeGuard+ instances. It is unclear whether these instances are excluded from final results. A separate development set or nested evaluation is needed.

No confidence intervals, task-level variance, hypothesis tests, or results across independent runs are reported. Generating 100 samples per task does not resolve uncertainty across only 94 CodeGuard+ tasks, and several reported differences are small enough that their reliability cannot be judged.

The component evidence is less consistent than the presentation suggests. For Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, vulnerability-cause retrieval alone obtains higher SecurePass@1 than all three facets, and removing sliced code at generation also improves SecurePass@1. Thus, the necessity of the complete design is not established uniformly.

The claimed novelty is primarily a combination of existing ingredients: CWE-based organization, LLM summarization, program slicing, query expansion through draft generation, dense/sparse retrieval, and thresholded RRF. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish the conceptual contribution from an application-specific engineering pipeline.

The program-analysis component is materially underspecified. Tree-sitter is named as the implementation basis, but the paper does not explain how sound data- and control-dependence graphs are constructed for Python, C, and C++, including aliasing, calls, scopes, and parsing failures. The vague cross-version context-completion step and fixed two-hop slicing rule further limit reproducibility.

The baseline comparison is difficult to interpret fairly. Several methods apply only to selected models, reimplementations change important components such as Codexity's analyzer, and extremely large functionality collapses for INDICT and CoSec suggest possible configuration mismatch. There is no comparison against simpler prompt baselines that receive the same generated vulnerability analysis or distilled guidelines without the full retrieval system.

The dynamic CWEval evaluation is valuable but substantially narrower than the main comparison: it includes only zero-shot and SecCoder, omits the other strong baselines, and does not report subset sizes, per-CWE results, uncertainty, or complete sampling details. Consequently, most comparative evidence still depends on CodeQL.

There is no audit for overlap or near-duplication between the SafeCoder-derived retrieval corpus and CodeGuard+/CWEval tasks. Reporting unseen CWE categories does not rule out overlap at the vulnerability, repository, patch, or code-pattern level.

The paper claims that functionality is retained, but Table 5 shows average Pass@1 decreases on CodeGuard+ and BigCodeBench. The aggregate '98.7%' statement obscures substantial model- and benchmark-specific regressions and should be accompanied by uncertainty and a clearer utility/cost analysis.

The offline cost of GPT-4o summarization, knowledge-base statistics, generated summaries, retrieval traces, and failure cases are insufficiently documented. The reproducibility statement refers to a repository link in the abstract, but no usable link is visible in the supplied manuscript.

Overall, the promising empirical signal does not yet overcome the test-set tuning, lack of statistical validation, limited novelty, and underspecified program-analysis implementation. These issues place the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold rather than supporting its state-of-the-art claims conclusively.

strengths: RESCUE presents a coherent and practically relevant framework that combines hierarchical security-knowledge construction, program slicing, and multi-faceted retrieval for secure code generation.
The evaluation is unusually broad: six LLMs, multiple model families and sizes, four main benchmarks, five representative baselines, and substantial sampling per task.

The central empirical result is convincing: RESCUE consistently improves the joint SecurePass@1 measure, including an average 6.28-point gain over zero-shot generation and a reported 4.8-point gain over the strongest competing method.

The ablations meaningfully examine knowledge-base construction, guidelines, program slicing, hierarchical retrieval, individual retrieval facets, fusion, and summarization models. Additional dynamic-testing, unseen-CWE, and cross-language experiments further strengthen the evidence.
The paper is well organized, technically plausible, and addresses the limitations and dual-use implications of the work.
weaknesses: The claim that security improves without compromising functional correctness is overstated. Table 5 reports average Pass@1 decreases of 2.7 points on CodeGuard+ and 3.63 points on BigCodeBench, with considerably larger drops for some model-benchmark pairs.

No confidence intervals, paired significance tests, or variation across independent runs are reported. This matters because several gains and ablation differences are modest and generation is stochastic.

The paper does not clearly establish instance-level independence between the SafeCoder-derived knowledge base and the evaluation benchmarks. Comparing only seen versus unseen CWE categories does not rule out duplicate or closely related vulnerabilities, projects, or code patterns.

Thresholds and the hierarchical top-k value appear selected using CodeGuard+ itself; the 20-task validation subset is not clearly separated from the final test results. This creates a risk of benchmark-specific tuning.

The method requires multiple additional LLM calls and roughly doubles or triples sequential latency, but there is no cost-normalized comparison with baselines or complete accounting of token/API cost. Describing the overhead as acceptable is therefore insufficiently supported.

Novelty is moderate rather than exceptional: the contribution mainly integrates established summarization, program slicing, hierarchical retrieval, and rank fusion techniques. Moreover, the dynamic CWEval comparison covers only zero-shot and SecCoder, rather than the full baseline set.

Reproducibility cannot be fully assessed because the manuscript's stated repository link is absent, and several implementation details needed to reconstruct the knowledge base and experimental splits are underspecified.
